Josh Downs is officially the most interesting case study in football right now.

Not because of what he is. Because of what 5 quarterbacks did to him, and what the 6th one is about to find out.

5 different quarterbacks have thrown him a touchdown. Daniel Jones 4, Anthony Richardson 3, Joe Flacco 2, Gardner Minshew 2, Philip Rivers 1.

Career: 231 catches, 2,494 yards, 12 touchdowns. Every yard of it in Indianapolis, none of it with a top 10 quarterback.

2023: 68 catches, 771 yards with Minshew. 2024: 72 catches, 803 yards with Richardson and Flacco. 
2025: 58 catches, 566 yards with Jones. 2026: 33 catches, 354 yards in 9 games with Jones.

With Anthony Richardson, 32 catches on 55 targets in 12 games. 58% on targets. With Flacco in 2024, 49 catches on 65 targets in 7 games. 75%. Same receiver, same routes. The only thing that changed was who threw it.

Flacco pace over 17 games: 119 catches, 1,102 yards.

Then the separation numbers.

Fantasy Points Data, 2025: 75.3 percent success rate against man coverage, 82nd percentile. 82.4 percent against press, 96th percentile.

2023 to 2025, 131 targets against man: 59 percent caught, 7.2 yards a target, plus 0.23 EPA a target. Against Cover 1, the look he sees most: 92 targets, plus 0.29 EPA a target.

2026: 2.97 yards of separation at the catch. 38 percent first read share, 97th percentile. Only 61.4 percent of his targets were even catchable.

Ian Hartitz, Fantasy Points Data: Downs ranks 5th of 104 receivers in average separation score. Xavier Worthy ranks 76th. Rashee Rice ranks 103rd.

Next Gen Stats: Downs 1.89 yards per route run against man, Rice 1.27. Against zone it flips. Rice 3.10, Downs 1.62.

Rice beats zone. Downs beats man. Mahomes finally has both at once.

And here is where the case study gets its second half. Mahomes elevates receivers. That is not a take, it is a pattern.

JuJu Smith-Schuster caught 78 passes for 933 yards in 2022, a career best 77.2 percent catch rate, second on the team behind Kelce. Mahomes threw for 5,250 yards that year and won the Super Bowl with JuJu, MVS, Justin Watson and Mecole Hardman. JuJu left, caught 29 passes for 260 yards in New England, and got released by the Giants.

Tyquan Thornton is the latest one. 11 catches, 219 yards, and a 154.9 passer rating when targeted. Mahomes completed 7 of 12 downfield passes for 285 yards in Thornton's final 3 healthy games.

Mahomes even said it himself about JuJu: he took for granted what JuJu did for him.

But there is a ceiling on the elevator, and it matters for Downs.

No Chiefs wide receiver has had a 1,000 yard season since Tyreek Hill left. JuJu came closest at 933 in 2022. Rice came closer at 938 as a rookie in 2023, and he missed the final game. Mahomes spreads the ball. Kelce is the real WR1, Walker eats targets, and the next man up eats the rest.

So Downs is now the cleanest test the league has ever run on Mahomes vs the analytics. The advanced numbers say he gets open better than almost anyone. The box score says he is a 5 foot 9 slot receiver who has never topped 803 yards. One of those two things was the quarterback. Sunday at Atlanta starts to answer which one.

Mahomes is throwing short, adapting to his personnel. 5.4 intended air yards per attempt. The Chiefs are 19th in passing yards and tied for 23rd with 16 completions of 20 or more yards. Thornton was the deep threat and he is out. Downs does not fix that. His average depth of target is 9.6 yards, 8th lowest in the league.

What he fixes is the thing defenses have been doing to KC all year: play man, take away the easy stuff, dare somebody to win. Nobody in that room could win. Now somebody can.

Concerns: Cover 0 eats him alive: 42 percent caught, 3.9 yards a target, minus 0.14 EPA. The drops are real: 5.0 percent drop rate this year. And Colts fans will tell you he quit on them in the last month.

Orlovsky said it on ESPN: "You can not cover Josh Downs in man coverage." Mina Kimes: "I really like this.

Time will tell.

NFL Week 10 Preview

Green Bay Packers vs. Minnesota Vikings

- Green Bay’s bludgeoning of the Patriots in New England last week was one of, if not the most impressive victory of the season across the whole league. I’m not surprised the Packers won, but I was not expecting them to hang 45 points on the Patriots. I’m very curious to see how Green Bay follows that up against the Vikings.

- Minnesota has more of a good than a great pass rush on its own, but Brian Flores’ pressure packages, and how he pairs coverage with his aggressive approach, is what gives the Vikings front an advantage in this game, even though Green Bay’s offensive line has been better over the past month.

- A month or so ago I called Christian Watson and Matthew Golden a top 5 WR duo in the league, and the two of them have been killing teams with big plays. What makes them specifically interesting against Minnesota is both of them can win on short to intermediate crossers against blitzes, they could both create margin on screens and either of them could win a one on one downfield where Watson, in particular, could be given a relative jump ball against a blitz, with one on one coverage. They are an interesting solve for Flores, as those are all key ways to beat a blitzing team, where I could actually see them essentially forcing Flores to back out of all the pressure he’s brought this season.

- Kirk Cousins is a veteran quarterback that has played for Kevin O’Connell, as well as with Justin Jefferson and the core of Minnesota’s pass catchers (even though T.J. Hockenson is out). Even though he’s joining the team this week he’s a major upgrade over Carson Wentz or Max Brosmer.

- This is the most interesting game on the slate, where I’m not going to overcount what happens in this contest, unless Jordan Love/ Watson/ Golden shred Minnesota.

Detroit Lions vs. New England Patriots (Munich)
- Drake Maye is a good NFL quarterback that can elevate a very mediocre group of pass catchers, as long as he’s not facing consistent, stacked pressure. How New England’s offensive line stacks up to Detroit’s front four is the key to this game.

- Another is how the Patriots’ normally very good secondary responds against Detroit’s loaded skill group, in the wake of last week’s aerial assault by Green Bay.

- Related, Jared Goff is my favorite example of a pressure sensitive quarterback. When he’s clean, he shreds, when he’s hit/ moved early and often, you can see his internal clock change.

Bengals vs. Steelers (Sunday Night Football)
- This game against the Steelers and Week 14 against the Chiefs, both home games for the Bengals, are the two toughest tests for 6-2 Cincinnati the rest of the way. That’s a prime reason I wrote up Joe Burrow to win the MVP weeks ago.

- Pittsburgh is coming off their bye, while the Bengals are coming off their victory against the Falcons in Madrid. Both teams have good looking injury situations for this late in the year.

- The Steelers’ clearest path to a victory here is if their pass rush is impactful, as I wouldn’t count on them winning another high scoring affair like their 30-27 win over Cincinnati in Week 3.

Dallas Cowboys vs. San Francisco 49ers
- Dallas has been a messy team this season that lost to Jalon Daniels’ Bucs in primetime, the Cardinals in overtime and they did everything they could to lose to the Daniel Jones Colts last week. Through the first 9 weeks, 4-5 Dallas was much closer to a bad team than a good one.

- However, if the Cowboys play a competitive game against the 49ers, that changes things some, as the NFC East is just about a free ticket to the postseason. Right now, Dallas looks like a slam dunk first round exit if they win the division, but a team that can play with the 49ers, could conceivably win a playoff game against anyone in the NFC.

- The biggest impediment to that outcome is Brock Purdy/ Kyle Shanahan’s offense could have a field day against this Cowboys defense, even though Mike Evans is still out.

- The second is that I don’t think the Cowboys’ offensive line is playing very well and the 49ers front four is a top 10, bordering on a top 5 unit with Nick Bosa and DeForest Buckner in the mix.

- The coaching disparity between these two teams is rather large.

Las Vegas Raiders vs. Seattle Seahawks
- Fernando Mendoza makes his first NFL start against one of, if not the league’s best defense in the Seahawks.

- The Seahawks front four is down one of their better players in Leonard Williams, but this is still a very good group aided by Mike Macdonald’s pressure packages.

- Raiders coach Klint Kubiak was Seattle’s offensive coordinator last year, so he’s very familiar with the Seahawks roster and how they operate. I’d think he tries to get Mendoza a few early layups, moves him around throughout the game and ultimately tries to keep him from having to drop back/ making him traditionally stand in the pocket while trying to identify where Seattle is bringing pressure for long stretches.

- Long term, I expect Mendoza to be a top 10 quarterback in the league and I don’t imagine he’ll be a +6.5 home underdog too many more times in his career.

- Sam Darnold is still out, which means Drew Lock gets another start.

- The left side of Seattle’s offensive line, LT Charles Cross and LG Quenton Nelson, make up arguably the best left side in the league and both of them are out.

- No one can really stop Jaxon Smith-Njigba, but I’d imagine he’s a particularly difficult draw for uncommon opponents like Vegas.

Atlanta Falcons vs. Kansas City Chiefs
- Especially in the wake of Atlanta trading away safety Jessie Bates, I’m a little surprised Kansas City is a flat 3-point favorite against the Falcons. Especially with Atlanta coming off a game played in Madrid.

- Patrick Mahomes is off the injury report, but Kenneth Walker is still questionable.

- Falcons edge James Pearce played last week, but I’ll be interested in seeing how he does against Kansas City, who isn’t very strong at offensive tackle, with his first game of the year under his belt.

- Atlanta has been a bit all over the road this year, with a decisive win against Green Bay while handing the 49ers their only loss of the season to date. The Falcons are coming off two pretty bad games against the Bucs and Bengals.

- After this game and next week against the Cardinals, the Chiefs have a brutal five game stretch: at Buf (TNF), at LAR (TNF), at Cin, vs. NE (MNF), vs. SF.

- That’s not a typo, the Chiefs have three road games in a row coming up, which will mark their third time this season where they have at least two road games in a row.

Tennessee Titans vs. Jacksonville Jaguars
- The Jaguars went all in, adding three players to their defense, including Bates and Eagles NT Jordan Davis, who both aren’t playing this week.

- Still, Jacksonville’s front will have a trench advantage against a Titans offensive line that has played much worse than they could have ever expected given the investments they’ve made in that group.

- The Titans are coming off their bye, where before that Cam Ward played his best game of the season (by far) against the Bengals, in an effort where he looked like a player that was taken with a first overall pick.

- The key to this game, and the rest of the Titans season, is seeing how often Ward plays at that level the rest of the way.

- For the Jaguars, Trevor Lawrence is a top 10 quarterback, one you could realistically argue is closer to 5 than 10. His supporting cast on offense is, I’ll continue to say, pretty average, but Tennessee is pretty thin on defense, with Jeffery Simmons in Chicago and Amani Hooker in Buffalo. Ward, with no Carnell Tate, playing well is Tennessee’s best shot to make this one interesting.

Jets vs. Bills
- The Jets have a complete skill group and a solid offensive line, giving them a fantastic foundation for a new future at quarterback.

- For those that claim sacks are a quarterback stat, Geno Smith is the poster child of that notion. If New York can manage Buffalo’s quality front four, the Jets are live here. If the Bills’ pass rush provides consistent disruption, Josh Allen and company could win with some distance, similar to how the Chiefs did against New York last week (even though that game was messy for Kansas City early).

- This looks like a good opportunity for Buffalo’s passing attack to show some ceiling.

Cleveland Browns vs. Houston Texans
- The Browns lost to the Saints last week after a full overtime period, in a game Shedeur Sanders played at quarterback.

- Deshaun Watson is back. I don’t think anyone is truly rooting for Watson, and I’m not sure any quarterback in the league has taken more unnecessary sacks than him this season, but he has had more positive moments this year than he’s otherwise had since leaving Houston.

- The Browns, who have a bottom tier offensive line, get pretty lucky here as Danielle Hunter is out and Will Anderson is still on the injury report. At full strength Houston’s pass rush could have completely derailed this game.

- C.J. Stroud is having a very good year, and he’s coming off a monster game against the Chargers where he threw for 384 yards and 5 scores.

- The Texans will be dangerous if they make the playoffs, but 3-5 Houston needs to stack wins to get there. This one looks like it will primarily be on Stroud given Houston’s reduced pass rush.

New Orleans Saints vs. Carolina Panthers
- There’s no nice way to say this, but I shoot from the hip, and this is an interesting game between two 3-5 teams that should not be playing for a division lead, which is what they’ll be doing come Sunday.

- Both teams have limited quarterbacks that have their moments, but probably aren’t guys you want to extend long term. Both teams have legitimate wide receiver 1’s. Both teams have solid, offensive-minded coaches that I’d call good, but are either of them good enough?

- Both teams also leave a lot to be desired on defense, with the caveat that Saints edge Chase Young is quietly having a very good season and the Panthers have been down both their perimeter corners for weeks.

- Saints left tackle Kelvin Banks returned last week and is off the injury report this week.

Arizona Cardinals vs. Los Angeles Rams
- Myles Garrett returned to action last week for the Rams, and he had 3 sacks against Washington.

- Carson Beck is making his first NFL start this week, and the Rams’ pass rush has a major trench advantage.

- Michael Wilson and Kendrick Bourne are on IR, giving Arizona an atrocious wide receiver room, with the caveat that tight end Trey McBride is good to go.

- Puka Nacua and Davante Adams are out, giving the Rams an equally atrocious wide receiver room.

- Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur was the Rams offensive coordinator from 2023 to 2025 (Sean McVay calls the offense)

Baltimore Ravens vs. Los Angeles Chargers (Monday Night Football)
- For those Ravens enthusiasts that said nasty things in response to me calling Joe Fagano the worst quarterback I’ve seen all year leading into last week’s game with the Jaguars, I accept your apology.

- Jacoby Brissett starts for Baltimore, giving them a radically better chance of being competitive than they were when forced to play Fagano.

- I’m real interested to see what kind of volume Zay Flowers sees this week.

- I’m not sure any team I’ve ever seen has had a worse first half of a season than the 2026 Los Angeles Chargers. The offensive line situation for the Chargers is genuinely bad in the interior, and that turned into a train wreck when they were down their two tackles. Justin Herbert played through a similar dynamic last year, and he still had his moments in a situation few would have. This year, that is not the case, to the point it reminds me of Jared Goff’s first season with Jeff Fisher.

- I don’t understand why the Chargers didn’t trade Khalil Mack.

- This is one of the few games left on the schedule where Los Angeles has a shot to win, but it will be very interesting to see how Jessie Minter treats Justin Herbert in this environment, considering that Minter was the Chargers defensive coordinator the past two seasons.

- Is this the most uninteresting Monday Night Football game in league history?

I have watched every NFL game for roughly a decade. I have done this for the purpose of sports speculation.

I run a reality-based program here.

Engagement is how I reach new users. So as long as engagement remains strong (comments/ shares) I’ll continue pumping this and similarly detailed insights out every week.

candidates.text:
My cousin works in the front office of a professional baseball team in Japan.

Every season, the team evaluates its foreign players on a standard form. Eight categories. The form was designed in 1987 and has never been changed. It was built to answer one question: will this American cause problems?

This year's American is a catcher from Oklahoma. Thirty-three. Slightly wider than our dugout door. Let's call him Lane.

My cousin let me translate his form.

1. PUNCTUALITY
Arrives two hours before every game. Not to train. To learn the names of the stadium staff. All 140 of them. He knows the parking attendant's daughter is applying to nursing school. We did not know this.

2. RESPECT FOR SENIORITY
Calls the 68-year-old groundskeeper "Mr. Enomoto, sir." Calls the team owner "Chief." Calls the owner's 91-year-old mother "young lady." She has attended every home game since.

3. TEAM HARMONY
Started a barbecue in the players' parking lot after every home win. Our backup shortstop, 22, has not spoken in a team meeting in three seasons. He now runs the grill. He has opinions about ribs. He shares them.

4. EMOTIONAL RESTRAINT
In August, our rookie hit his first walk-off home run. The first player out of the dugout was Lane. Crying. He was not involved in the play. He was involved emotionally.

5. LANGUAGE EFFORT
Speaks 41 words of Japanese. 30 are food. Says "arigato" to the umpire after strike three. The umpires held a meeting about this. They have decided they like it.

6. FAN RELATIONS
Signs every autograph. Every single one. After a loss in July, he stayed two hours in the rain. A security guard held an umbrella over him. A second guard held an umbrella over the first guard. A third guard went for coffee.

7. CONDUCT TOWARD OPPONENTS
Tipped his cap to a pitcher who struck him out. The pitcher's mother wrote us a letter. We have no procedure for this letter. It is in a drawer.

8. ADDITIONAL REMARKS
Our rookie is Kaisei. He is 20. His father had not missed a home game since Kaisei signed. Three hours each way. Section 14, row 3. He always brought the same banner, made from an old tablecloth, with Kaisei's name painted on it in big, shaky letters.

In June, his father died suddenly.

Lane does not understand Buddhist funerals. He went anyway. He bought a black suit that morning. It was the biggest one in the store, and it was still too small. He took the last seat in the last row.

When it was his turn to offer incense, he froze. He didn't know how.

Kaisei's little brother, who is nine, came down the aisle to the last row, took Lane's huge hand, and showed him. Pinch. Lift to the forehead. Drop. Bow.

Lane did it exactly the way he was taught. Then he stayed for all three hours.

At the end, he gave Kaisei his bat. The one he hit his first home run in Japan with.

"Your dad's got a better view than any of us now," he said. "Every at-bat. Let's give him something to watch."

The next home game, there was something new hanging in our dugout. An old tablecloth. Kaisei's name in big, shaky letters.

Lane had asked the family if he could borrow it. He hung it himself before every game until the season ended. Nobody told him to.

Kaisei batted .310 from June on. With that bat.

The walk-off in August, the one Lane cried about? That was Kaisei. That was the bat. Rounding third, Kaisei pointed at the dugout. Not at the crowd. At the tablecloth.

The form ends with one last box. RECOMMEND CONTRACT RENEWAL: YES / NO.

For 39 years, the general manager has circled one word and filed it.

This year, somebody turned the form over.

Twenty-eight signatures. The entire roster. The backup shortstop. Kaisei, in very large letters. Mr. Enomoto, the groundskeeper, who is not on the roster and was not asked. A very careful pencil signature from a nine-year-old, who is also not on the roster. And Kaisei's mother, who mailed hers in a separate envelope and asked that it please be stapled on.

Under all of them, one word in English, in the groundskeeper's handwriting:

"PLEASE."

Lane signed for two more years.

The form has still never been changed. But my cousin says that next season, they're adding a ninth category.

It doesn't have a name yet. They're calling it "the Lane thing."

America, you sent us a catcher.

You don't fit on any of our forms.

Please keep sending people who don't.

Micah Parsons wanted his agent to finish his new contract. Jerry Jones said they already had a deal, refused to start over, and traded him to Green Bay. The Packers gave him a $188 million contract.

The agent Jones wouldn't negotiate with is the one who closed it.

In the video below, Parsons at Cowboys camp in July 2025 says other teams are "taking care of their best guys." After the trade, Jones says "There's no question that I could have signed him in April," and that an agent "isn't necessarily anywhere to be found 10 years later."

In the spring of 2025, Parsons met Jones for what he says was a talk about leadership. Jones says they agreed on "term, amounts, guarantees, everything," and then the agent told him not to bother.

That agent, David Mulugheta, later said the offer averaged $40.5 million a year, but in the first three years it would not have made Parsons the top-paid player.

Parsons asked for a trade on Aug. 1. At the last preseason game he lay on a medical table behind the bench, his Cowboys jacket turned inside out.

On Aug. 28, Dallas sent him to Green Bay for two first-round picks and defensive tackle Kenny Clark. His Packers deal runs four years with $136 million guaranteed and made him the highest-paid non-quarterback in NFL history.

For Jones: he says his offer had more guaranteed money than any defensive player had ever gotten, and he still got two first-round picks.

For Parsons: using an agent is standard, and Mulugheta says he reached out to the Cowboys "numerous times" to start talks.

Asked whether Jerry or Stephen Jones told him about the trade, Parsons said: "It was pretty much all through David."

So did Jerry Jones lose Micah Parsons over an agent, or did Parsons back out of a deal he had already made?
